attacks.claim: TRAILING_PUNCT strips every trailing ')' from a matched URL, so a link that legitimately ends in a parenthesis (e.g. Wikipedia-style 'Drill_(tool)') becomes a broken URL. This is a common linkifier heuristic, and the test deliberately covers the sentence-punctuation case.

The trailing-punctuation regex can take quadratic time on a very long run of punctuation inside a matched URL. This needs an extreme, deliberately crafted description (tens of thousands of characters), so it is not blocking.

A leading link longer than the limit is shown whole, so the collapsed view can stay tall and a long unbroken URL may overflow on narrow screens. This is an intentional, commented trade-off and affects only a rare case.
attacks.evidence: else if (out.length === 0) { out.push(t); // a leading link is shown whole rather than collapsing to nothing

attacks.claim: The PR text and test title say truncation never splits a word, but the hard-cut fallback for an unbroken 400-character string cuts mid-word. The limit also mixes UTF-16 code units with code points.
attacks.evidence: test('truncation never splits a link or a word' ... expect(truncate(tokenize('x'.repeat(400)), 280)
